newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government, Chirac agree on NATO -Richard.
newsitem.headline: French government, Chirac agree on NATO -Richard.

text.p: Defence Minister Alain Richard said on Wednesday that France's leftist government and conservative President Jacques Chirac agreed on a decision taken at a NATO summit not to return to the alliance's military command.
"There was no compromise -- this is a point on which we were in agreement with the president - on France's eventual return to the NATO military structures," Richard said in a broadcast interview.
"There was an agreement not to accept the final American proposals, which in fact did not recognise Europe's collective contribution as an alliance asset," he said on Europe 1 radio.

Chirac, speaking at the Madrid summit on Tuesday, had similarly insisted he had made no concession so far on rejoining the integrated military command, which Paris left in 1966 in protest at U.S. domination of the alliance.
U.S. President Bill Clinton called at the summit for new negotiations between NATO and France with the aim of bringing Paris back into the integrated command by the end of the year.
But he again rejected Chirac's key demand that Washington hand over NATO's Naples-based southern command to a European.
Diplomats quoted Clinton as saying Washington wanted France to have a full place in the integrated structure but the new command arrangements had to make military sense.

The question of possible internal French differences on the issue had been raised ahead of the summit when the government announced, without mentioning the president's views, that Paris was giving up on the initiative, which had been launched by Chirac before the left came to power.

After two years of working with a rightist government, Chirac is now obliged to share power with the government led by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin. The right was swept from power in an upset June 1 parliamentary election.

Richard, in the interview, also said that the government and Chirac both supported a French summit compromise which enabled just three Eastern European states to enter NATO, in line with Washington's wishes, rather than five, as Paris had sought.
Richard said it was "logical" that there would be differences between the Right and the Left on defence policy.

However he played down their importance on a variety of issues now under debate, ranging from the defence budget to the possible privatisation of defence firms an ongoing reform of the French armed forces.
In France, where anti-American rhetoric is a political staple, there have been domestic political doubts all along about Chirac's initiative to negotiate France's return to the NATO military command.
Since taking power, the Jospin government has been particularly outspoken against U.S. "hegemony" in world affairs.
Richard said the outcome of the NATO summit would now give new momentum to drives to create a distinct European defence identity and a single European voice on foreign policy.
"We favour the development of European foreign policy and defence functions...We must review ways to make concrete progress in establishing European responsibility for security and defence," he said.
